articles.title: Elon Musk is absolutely not a ‘free speech absolutist’
articles.summary: Elon Musk has accused Brazil’s government of “censoring” free speech, but he’s enabled other regimes’ efforts at doing so.
articles.body: Elon Musk is a self-proclaimed “free speech absolutist.” He’s declared himself so committed to the unfettered, open exchange of ideas that he’s said the only way X would let a government suppress speech on its platform is “at gunpoint.” All of this explains why Musk recently allowed X to be banned in Brazil rather than comply with the country’s mandate that the social media platform block certain accounts. It does far less to explain Musk’s history of doing that very thing in other countries — often at the behest of right-wing or authoritarian regimes. [Media: Musk has been open to following government orders from nearly the beginning. In January 2023 — a little over two months after Musk’s takeover — the platform then known as Twitter blocked a BBC documentary critical of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi. India’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting confirmed that Twitter was among the platforms that suppressed The Modi Question at the behest of the Modi government, which called the film “hostile propaganda and anti-India garbage.” Musk later claimed he had no knowledge of this. But in March, after the Indian government imposed an internet blackout on the northern state of Punjab, Twitter caved again. It suppressed Indian users’ access to more than 100 accounts belonging to prominent activists, journalists, and politicians, The Intercept reported at the time. Later that year, Twitter’s Global Government Affairs account announced it had “taken actions to restrict some content in Turkey” to ensure the website “remains available to the people of Turkey.” As Slate noted at the time, Twitter imposed restrictions on certain accounts on the eve of Turkey’s national elections — and it did so amid rampant social media criticism of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. --- * January 2023 - Germany: X was sued for allegedly failing to properly moderate antisemitic content and Holocaust denial on its platform. * January 2023 - India: X suppressed a BBC documentary critical of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. * March 2023 - India: X blocked users from viewing over 100 accounts belonging to prominent opponents of the Modi government. * May 2023 - Turkey: X complied with court orders to block certain accounts and posts. * April 2024 - Australia: Musk accused the country of “censorship” after a judge ordered X to block a video showing a bishop being stabbed in a Sydney church. --- Twitter representatives later said the company had filed objections to court orders requiring the website to ban access to some posts and accounts. Still, Twitter suppressed the accounts and posts. “We received what we believed to be a final threat to throttle the service — after several such warnings,” Twitter said in a statement, adding it “took action” on four accounts and 409 tweets “in order to keep Twitter available over the election weekend.” Musk has previously said that despite his personal beliefs about free speech, his “preference is to hew close to the laws of countries in which Twitter operates.” In a 2023 interview with the BBC, Musk said Twitter “can’t go beyond the laws” of the countries in which it operates. He reiterated the claim in an interview with CNN, in which he said the platform has “no actual choice” but to comply with government censorship requests. [Media: Under Musk, the website now known as X has complied with such requests readily. Between October 2022 and April 2023, Twitter received 971 requests from governments and courts to suppress specific content and identify private information about anonymous accounts, according to Lumen data analyzed by Rest of World. It complied, to some degree, with 99 percent of those. The majority of these requests came from countries with restrictive speech laws, including India, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates. But X isn’t always amenable to government moderation requests, nor is it particularly vigilant about removing illegal content. In January 2023, a European anti-hate speech group filed a lawsuit in Germany, alleging the platform had failed to properly moderate antisemitic content and Holocaust denial on its platform, violating both its own policies and German law. There has been a marked rise in hate speech on X since Musk’s takeover, due in no small part to Musk’s decision to fire the content moderation team and X’s Trust and Safety Council. Musk has also been at odds with European Union regulators over disinformation on X. In 2022, Musk said he was “very much on the same page” as the EU regarding the Digital Services Act (DSA), a far-reaching law that requires major online platforms to remove posts containing illegal content and holds them legally accountable if they don’t. But the following year, X pulled out of the EU’s voluntary Code of Practice against disinformation, a voluntary agreement that in effect functioned as a precursor to the DSA. EU regulators have since criticized X for allowing disinformation and illegal content to remain on the platform, and EU Commissioner Thierry Breton has warned Musk that regulators are keeping tabs on the platform. Musk has, for his part, occasionally antagonized Breton and the EU regulators over their stance on X. This April, after an Australian judge ruled that X was required to block a video showing a bishop being stabbed in a Sydney church, Musk accused the country of censorship. X’s Global Government Affairs account said the company believed the order “was not within the scope of Australian law” and said the country “does not have the authority to dictate what content X’s users can see globally.” Some of the inconsistencies in X’s compliance with government censorship requests could be attributed to technicalities. (X did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment on its decisions.) Turkey and India requested that it suppress content only in their countries, while Australia tried to censor a video globally. But it’s worth noting that the video played into one of Musk’s pet causes: combating the so-called “great replacement” of white people by immigrants and people of color. Australian authorities said they believed the stabbing was a religiously motivated terrorist attack. More broadly, Musk has a history of antagonizing governments and politicians he considers too “woke.” Musk’s other business interests may also be relevant. Erdoğan asked Musk to build a Tesla factory in Turkey last fall, just a few months after X suppressed critics’ posts. And this April, the Financial Times reported that Tesla is exploring locations for a $3 billion factory in India. The man who once said he’d only allow one of his companies to suppress speech “at gunpoint” is far less firm in his beliefs than he claims.

articles.title: Trump is waging a silent war on legal immigration
articles.summary: ICE raids are the most visible attack on undocumented communities, but through the DOJ and USCIS, Trump has quietly wielded bureaucracy against legal immigrants, too.
articles.body: When the member states of the United Nations reviewed their Global Compact on Migration earlier this month, one country was conspicuously absent from the discussions: the United States. In a post on X explaining its reasoning, the State Department said it objects to global “efforts to facilitate replacement migration to the United States and our Western allies.” A subsequent post clarified that President Donald Trump’s administration supports “remigration — but not replacement migration.” If “replacement migration” sounds like a dogwhistle, that’s because it’s one the administration’s loudest ones yet. Such allusions to the “great replacement” — a far-right conspiracy theory that a cabal of global elites is importing people of color to the US as a means of demographic warfare — and support of remigration, the notion that immigrants and their descendants should be returned to their countries of origin regardless of citizenship voluntarily or otherwise, were once limited to the fringes of the far right. Now they are coming from the government itself. (Elon Musk, a longtime proponent of the great replacement theory, applauded the State Department’s “banger thread.”) Eliminating “replacement migration” and pushing “remigration” are hallmarks of Trump’s second-term immigration policy, which has focused on deporting as many people as possible while preventing new immigrants from arriving here. It’d be easier to ignore if it was just a post on X. But since returning to office, Trump has drastically slashed legal immigration and has worked to strip immigrants of their legal status in pursuit of his mass deportation policy. Where Trump once promised to go after the so-called “bad hombres” coming to the US illegally, Trump’s aggressive second-term immigration policies suggest that all noncitizens are fair game. For years, proponents of hardline immigration policies have said that the problem isn’t immigration itself, just the fact that some people come to America the “wrong” way. But Trump’s crackdown on legal immigration fulfills the far-right’s dream of racial exclusion. A recent report by the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, found that Trump has cut legal immigration more than illegal immigration. Unauthorized migration fell by over 80 percent in the final year of Joe Biden’s term, the report found. By the time Trump was back in the White House, border crossings were already at historic lows — lower, in fact, than when he left office in 2021. The drop in legal immigration, on the other hand, is largely a product of Trump’s own making. “When he came in, he was really able to do whatever he wanted, because the flows were already so reduced,” David Bier, the director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute and author of the report, told The Verge. Bier found that 132,000 fewer people are being admitted to the US each month under Trump. And unlike Trump’s suspension of asylum at the border — which a federal appeals court recently ruled illegal — the sharp reduction in legal immigration isn’t the product of a single policy. While much of the public’s attention is on the Department of Homeland Security’s shock-and-awe raids in American cities, the Trump administration has waged a quiet war on legal immigration through a patchwork of executive orders and regulatory changes. The first year of Trump’s second term in office saw a net decline in migration for the first time in decades. Population growth slowed as a result, according to Census Bureau data. The decline in net migration will weaken the economy, according to researchers at the Brookings Institution and the American Enterprise Institute, both of which lean right. “Such weakness is the new normal under the current immigration policy,” the report found, “rather than weakness reflecting adverse business cycle conditions.” Migration numbers will likely drop further in 2026. Last December, Trump banned the issuance of immigrant visas to nationals of 40 countries, including the Palestinian territories, to “prevent national security and public safety threats from reaching our borders.” The White House claimed that these nations, most of which were in Africa, had “deficient screening and vetting information” for prospective emigrants. The ban affected 20 percent of all visa applicants, and didn’t include a waiver for the spouses, minor children, or parents of US citizens and permanent residents. The White House also implemented a ban on non-immigrant visas — such as those issued to tourists or students — for nationals of some of the affected countries, including Nigeria and Venezuela. In January, the administration suspended immigrant visas for 75 countries (some of which were already affected by the previous ban), claiming that people from them were “nationalities at high risk of public benefits usage” and would thus be a burden on US taxpayers. “We are working to ensure that the generosity of the American people will no longer be abused,” the State Department said in a post on X. The administration’s rationale for this latter ban was the public charge rule, which originated in the 19th century. Since 1882, US law has denied entry to prospective immigrants deemed “unable to take care of himself or herself without becoming a public charge.” The statutory language has changed since then, but the practice remains — and has expanded under Trump, who has a habit of using very old legislation as threadbare justification for his new policies. This ban affected nearly half of all applicants, according to a lawsuit filed by a coalition of organizations led by the Catholic Legal Immigration Network. They alleged that the visa suspension was “based on unsupported and demonstrably false claims that the nationals of the covered countries migrate to the United States to improperly rely on cash welfare.” In fact, many immigrants are ineligible for such benefits. The suit also claimed that the State Department implemented “new, discriminatory rules” regarding public charge that broke from established precedent. More recently, the State Department ordered consular officers abroad to ask visa applicants whether they fear going back to their home country. This change was implemented after a federal court determined that the Trump administration’s shutdown of asylum at the southern border was illegal. To obtain humanitarian protections like asylum, a person must prove that they face persecution in their country due to their race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership in a particular social group. Since April, consular officers have been instructed to ask all visa applicants two questions: “Have you experienced harm or mistreatment in your country of nationality or last habitual residence?” and “Do you fear harm or mistreatment in returning to your country of nationality or permanent residence?” If a person says yes to either, their visa is denied. If they say no and later ask for asylum in the US, their previous statements can be used against them in deportation hearings. “They’re trying to systematically demolish any means by which a persecuted person could seek protection and safety in the United States,” Jeremy Konyndyk, the president of Refugees International, told The Washington Post, which first reported on the new policy. Refugee admissions are also down, dropping by 90 percent in Trump’s second term, according to the Cato report. Trump set the cap on refugee resettlement for the 2026 fiscal year to just 7,500 people. The administration is reportedly considering doubling that number — but only for the benefit of one group. According to documents obtained by The New York Times, the Trump administration is hoping to resettle more white Afrikaners in the United States. Since Trump’s return to office, members of the white South African minority are effectively the only group to be resettled in the United States. Trump’s attacks on legal immigration don’t just affect people seeking to travel or migrate to the United States. The first visa ban, which was issued under a national security rationale, has also led to the pausing or reversal of work authorizations for some immigrants already living in the United States. One cancer researcher from Myanmar, who has lived in the country since 2016, told NPR she is now unable to work as a result. A medical student originally from Nigeria who has been in the US since 2011 can no longer fulfill her surgery residency. Like the fee increase for H-1B visas to $100,000, the travel ban is preventing immigrants from working in key industries, many of which are facing labor shortages. The administration has also stripped immigrants of their legal status. In April, the Supreme Court heard arguments over Trump’s decision to rescind Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Syria and Haiti. TPS is a conditional shield from deportation issued to nationals of certain countries after emergencies, such as armed conflicts or natural disasters. For example, after the Obama administration designated TPS for those affected by the Syrian civil war, Syrians already present in the US could apply for TPS to obtain a work permit and be shielded from deportation. Unlike asylum and refugee status, TPS doesn’t lead to a green card or path to citizenship. Like Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals — another policy the Trump administration has sought to end — TPS is a sort of legal limbo, albeit one that provides a modicum of stability for immigrants who would otherwise be undocumented. Trump’s efforts to rescind TPS and terminate DACA are part of a broader effort to expand the pool of who is deportable. “The narrative that has been put forth by the administration is, ‘We’re going to go after criminals, we’re going to go after people who are here without authorization,’” Astrid Liden, a communications officer at the Hope Border Institute, told The Verge. In reality, she said, the policy is, “We’re going to go after those without authorization, but if you have authorization, we’re going to take it away to make you deportable.” Asylum agents with US Citizenship and Immigration Services, the agency that handles legal immigration, has been instructed to find evidence of rampant fraud within the asylum system, one former employee told The New Yorker — and were chastised when their research proved the opposite. Under Trump, the budget for USCIS’s Fraud Detection and National Security division more than doubled. USCIS has indefinitely frozen green card processing for nationals of countries subject to travel bans, and the agency has begun retroactively stripping refugees of their status once they apply for permanent residency. Administration officials have signaled that these policies will soon expand beyond noncitizens. At the recent Border Security Expo in Phoenix, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said the administration will aggressively pursue denaturalization cases. The New York Times reported that the Department of Justice is aiming to strip 200 people of their citizenship each month. Trump’s attempt to eliminate birthright citizenship via executive order was taken up by the Supreme Court last month. If the administration succeeds, it would leave hundreds of thousands of children essentially stateless upon birth — and immediately eligible for deportation. Bier, of the Cato Institute, said that eliminating birthright citizenship would also make it easier to deport immigrants who can no longer ask for relief because they’re the parents of US citizen children. And it would make it harder for anyone to use their birth certificate as proof of US citizenship. Even now, proof of citizenship isn’t enough to prevent Americans from being arrested by ICE. Leonardo Garcia Venegas, a US citizen who was born in Florida, has been detained by DHS three times in the past year, according to ProPublica. Garcia Venegas, who has since filed a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration ordering ICE to stop raids in his area, is reportedly considering moving to his family’s home in Mexico. “I just want to live in peace,” he told the outlet. The administration has acknowledged that DHS occasionally arrests US citizens — and officials have doubled down. “I’m not going to do anything to not arrest US citizens,” Customs and Border Protection chief Rodney Scott said at the border security conference. “Because we arrest criminals, period.” That’s the crux of remigration: to make life so unbearable for immigrants and their children that they “choose” to leave. “It’s all connected. They don’t want people to come here legally, because if they come here legally, then they won’t be able to be deported as easily. And getting rid of people’s legal status — whether it’s Temporary Protected Status or parole, or whatever temporary visas they have — that’s an essential component of increasing the number of arrests and deportations,” Bier said. “That is the core of their strategy: ramping up these arrests and making it more difficult for people to stay here.”

articles.title: Innocent woman says police use of Flock camera led to 13 days in jail
articles.summary: Lindsey Brooke Isaacs spent 13 days in jail after a Flock camera flagged her Dodge Durango near a fatal Florida crash that killed three people.
articles.body: Lindsey Brooke Isaacs was asleep at home when police arrived and told the 23-year-old that her car had been involved in a crash that killed three people. She knew they had the wrong person. Her black Dodge Durango showed no obvious collision damage, and she had a receipt showing where she had been. Still, the investigation eventually led to her being arrested and 13 days in jail. "My heart was in my stomach," Lindsey told me on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/. "I didn't know what was going on." Months later, prosecutors dropped all eight felony charges against her and investigators arrested another woman in connection with the crash. Her case now raises a bigger question about how much weight investigators should give license plate camera data when a person's freedom is on the line. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE How a Flock camera became a major lead The deadly crash happened on Oct. 4, 2025, along eastbound Interstate 4 near DeBary, Florida. Motorcyclist Joaquin Deno died. Flagler County Deputy Administrator Jorge Salinas and his wife, Nancy Salinas, also died. Witnesses reported that a Dodge Durango was involved. Investigators found Lindsey's black Dodge Durango through a Flock automated license plate reader. The camera recorded her vehicle traveling eastbound near the Seminole and Volusia county line at 9:51 p.m. That camera was about three miles west of the crash scene. The crash happened around 9:53 p.m. That timing became especially important later. Lindsey's attorney, Patrick McGeehan, said his team performed a time-distance analysis and concluded Lindsey was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. So the camera really did capture Lindsey's vehicle. The problem came from what investigators concluded from that sighting. Lindsey put it more bluntly during our conversation. "They just picked up my car off a camera and called it the end of the day. We got her." Other evidence pointed toward a different Dodge Durango The Flock camera hit was far from the only information investigators had. A 911 caller described a maroon Dodge Durango and provided part of its license plate number. Later, investigators also found red or maroon paint transfer on a Ford Focus involved in the crash. Meanwhile, Lindsey drove a black Dodge Durango. A specialized Florida Highway Patrol team later inspected Lindsey's vehicle and reported finding no damage suggesting it had been involved in a collision with another vehicle. That finding lined up with something Lindsey said she had been telling investigators from the beginning. "Where is the damage on the vehicle?" she recalled asking police. "Because I'm standing right in front of it and I don't see any damage." Still, authorities impounded her SUV. Months passed. Lindsey Isaacs is arrested on charges seven months later On April 17, 2026, Lindsey got a call from her attorney. She had to surrender that day. "They are arresting you for this crime," Lindsey recalled him telling her. She faced eight felony charges: three counts of vehicular homicide, three counts of leaving the scene of a crash involving death, leaving the scene involving serious bodily injury and reckless driving causing serious bodily injury. Lindsey spent 13 days in jail. During our podcast conversation, she described spending her first several days in solitary confinement. She said she had a toilet, a sink and a metal sleeping slab covered by a thin mat. Her charges were so serious, she said, that jail officials initially kept her separated from other people. Later, Lindsey was transferred to other sections of the jail. After her first bond hearing, she remained behind bars. "I was devastated, I was scared," she told me. "I thought my life was over." HOW SURVEILLANCE TECH LED POLICE TO ACCUSE THE WRONG PERSON A new investigation changes the case The case finally began moving in a very different direction after prosecutors and a specialized Florida Highway Patrol team took another look. That team found no meaningful crash damage on Lindsey's Durango. Investigators revisited witness information and followed evidence pointing toward another vehicle. On May 22, the State Attorney's Office formally declined to prosecute Lindsey on all eight charges. Authorities then arrested Alisa Lee Montalvo on charges connected to the crash. Prosecutors allege Montalvo was driving a maroon Dodge Durango. She faces nine charges, including three counts of vehicular homicide and tampering with physical evidence. She has not been convicted, and the charges remain allegations. For Lindsey, the news brought enormous relief. "I felt like a new woman," she told me. "I felt free." Lindsey told me she later received an apology from the head of the Florida Highway Patrol. "It felt like a miracle," she said. "Another miracle from God that I was hearing it in person, face to face." However, she also said the experience left lasting emotional and physical effects. "This took and is going to take maybe years to get better mentally, physically, emotionally," Lindsey said. Lindsey has since filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against two Florida Highway Patrol troopers involved in the investigation, alleging false arrest, wrongful imprisonment and malicious prosecution. Those claims have not been proven in court. Flock Safety responds We reached out to Flock Safety and the Florida Highway Patrol for comment. Flock Safety responded with the following statement: "Flock cameras provide investigative leads; they do not identify perpetrators, determine guilt, or make arrest decisions. In fact, the complaint itself calls the Flock evidence 'exculpatory, not inculpatory,' meaning the evidence pointed away from Ms. Isaacs rather than implicating her: it accurately placed her vehicle three miles from the crash scene just two minutes before the crash. Characterizing her arrest as the result of Flock technology fundamentally misrepresents both the allegations and the role our technology played in this case." The Florida Highway Patrol did not respond to our request for comment. What a Flock camera can record Flock cameras are automated license plate readers, often called ALPRs. They capture images of passing vehicles and use software to identify license plates. Flock systems can also capture vehicle characteristics including make, model and color. Each camera sighting can create a record linking a vehicle with a particular place and time. For police, that can become an extremely useful investigative tool. A stolen car can appear on a camera. A vehicle connected to a missing person case could produce a lead. However, Lindsey's experience raises another question. What happens when investigators put too much confidence in one search result? We previously explored that concern after surveillance technology helped police accuse a Colorado woman of stealing a package. Her own phone location history eventually helped show where she had really been. Lindsey blames how investigators used the Flock data One of the most interesting moments in my conversation with Lindsey came when I asked whether she blamed the Flock technology or the way police interpreted its data. Her answer was clear. "I 100% think the second one you said, how police interpret the camera footage," she told me. That gets to the heart of this story. The Flock camera captured Lindsey's vehicle traveling on I-4. The machine did what it was designed to do. Human judgment came next. Investigators had to decide what that sighting meant. They also had to weigh it against witness accounts, physical evidence and the condition of Lindsey's car. According to Lindsey's federal complaint, the Flock hit three miles from the crash two minutes beforehand, ultimately helped her legal team argue that she was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. Technology can surface a lead. People still have to prove what that lead actually means. FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES Florida orders license plate readers off state highways The debate over these cameras has now taken a major turn in Florida. On Aug. 31, the Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for license plate reader systems within rights-of-way on Florida's state highway system. FDOT cited the rapid growth of the systems along with reports of misuse and concerns involving data privacy and surveillance. Cameras covered by the order must be removed within 30 days. The agency also said it will stop issuing future permits for license plate readers within its jurisdiction. However, that order does not eliminate every Flock camera in Florida. It applies to cameras within FDOT-controlled state highway rights of way. Local governments can take different approaches to cameras on city or county property. Several agencies have chosen to pull back further. Miami-Dade County, for example, announced that it would suspend its entire license plate reader program. Other Florida agencies plan to continue using cameras away from state highways. Flock is adding new safeguards Flock Safety has also announced significant changes to how its system operates. In August, the company announced that it was changing its recommended and default license plate data retention period from 30 days to seven days. Flock also plans to require law enforcement customers to use its Audit Assistance tool by the end of 2026. The technology flags unusual search activity for review. Case codes will also become mandatory for law enforcement searches by the end of the year. Flock says emergency searches can bypass that requirement, although those searches will be flagged for review. Those changes add oversight. Still, safeguards inside the software cannot determine whether an investigator has drawn the right conclusion from the information on the screen. Your license plate can create a trail Most of us probably drive past license plate readers without noticing them. A single plate scan may seem harmless. After all, anyone standing beside the road can see your license plate. A searchable network changes the equation. Instead of someone seeing your vehicle once, a network of cameras can record when that vehicle passed particular locations. We have already reported on Flock license plate cameras appearing at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots. We also reported on a Washington court ruling that found Flock license plate reader images can qualify as public records under that state's Public Records Act. Lindsey told me she knew Flock cameras existed before her ordeal. She simply had no idea how much could ride on the information they collected. "I just thought it was like a traffic camera," she said. Today, her opinion has changed. "I feel very different about those cameras now." POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN' What to do if police connect your vehicle to an investigation If police tell you that your vehicle appeared in a license plate reader search tied to a serious crime, your own records could become important. 1) Preserve your location records Save receipts and toll records that can help establish where you were. If your phone already stores location history, preserve that information too. Avoid changing or deleting anything related to the period investigators are asking about. 2) Save camera footage quickly Doorbell cameras and security systems often overwrite older recordings. If footage could show your vehicle at home or somewhere else, preserve a copy as soon as possible. The same goes for dashcam video. 3) Photograph and video your vehicle If authorities claim your car was involved in a collision, take detailed pictures and video showing its condition. Photograph and record each side of the vehicle and keep the original files with their date information intact. 4) Consider contacting an attorney A serious criminal accusation can escalate quickly. An attorney can help preserve evidence and communicate with investigators. Legal counsel can also examine whether the available data actually supports what police believe happened. Kurt's key takeaways I'm torn on Flock cameras. If somebody burglarizes my home, I want police to have technology that can help identify the vehicle that drove away. If investigators are trying to locate a missing person, a license plate reader could provide a valuable lead. But Lindsey's story shows what can happen when a lead begins driving the investigation instead of helping investigators test what really happened. Her black Dodge Durango had no crash damage. Other evidence pointed toward a maroon Durango. The timing of the Flock hit ultimately helped her attorney argue that she could not have caused the crash. Yet she still spent 13 days in jail. As I told Lindsey during our conversation, "I can't stand when technology is used in ways that it was never intended for." That is where I land on this. The technology can be incredibly useful. The people using it still need to challenge what they think they know before someone loses their freedom. For more of Lindsey's remarkable firsthand account, listen to or watch my full conversation with her on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/. After hearing what happened to Lindsey, would you want Flock cameras in your community, or has this case changed how you feel about police tracking license plates? articles.title: US Treasury Triples Long-Dated Debt Buyback to $6 Billion
articles.summary: The US Treasury said it will purchase up to $6 billion of longer-dated government debt in the first operation under an expanded buybacks program, showcasing...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The US Treasury said it will purchase up to $6 billion of longer-dated government debt in the first operation under an expanded buybacks program, showcasing Secretary Scott Bessent's resolve to stem the recent rise in borrowing costs.

The maximum size is triple the amount initially communicated to investors of $2 billion. That plan was discarded in a surprise Aug. 19 announcement, when the Treasury said it would "at least double" the size of such operations.

Some dealers had ramped up their predictions for Thursday's buyback operation after Bessent publicly touted the potential for purchases of over $4 billion. The Treasury chief on Tuesday reiterated that while he cannot alter the "equilibrium" price of Treasuries, his objective was to slow moves down and prevent any damaging narrative taking hold in the world's biggest bond market.

Treasuries extended an earlier decline after the release, with the yield on 10-year notes up about 6 basis points to 4.85% as of 11:16 a.m. in New York.

The market reaction shows how some investors had expected an even-larger operation. Guneet Dhingra, BNP Paribas SA's head of US rates strategy, said before the announcement it would take a maximum size of $7 billion to surprise the market, with anything less triggering selling pressure.

How successful the enlarged program will prove remains to be seen. Yields dropped after the initial announcement of the plan last month, but retraced the move. Benchmark 10-year yields last week hit their highest since 2023.

Markets in August, when 30-year yields hit their highest since 2007, were driven by concerns "the US is not going to be able to pay its debt. It was absurd, but it just became kind of the dominant narrative," Bessent claimed in a Texas event. He has separately characterized buybacks as aimed at boosting liquidity. They will enable banks and other institutions to offload harder-to-trade securities so that they can then boost their participation in auctions of new debt, he said last week.

"Scott has absolutely adopted a very activist model as Treasury secretary," Krishna Guha, head of economics at Evercore ISI, said before Wednesday's announcement. "He's tactically very skilled in terms of when and how to surprise and move markets and has had some near-term success."

articles.title: Treasury poised to buy up to $6B in bonds as Bessent looks to rein in debt costs
articles.summary: The Treasury secretary is aiming to project strength as he seeks to sway markets. “I am the house now,” he said at an event Tuesday. “Bet against me if you w...
articles.body:
The Treasury Department announced Wednesday that the federal government will buy back up to $6 billion of its bonds this week — triple the size of its normal operations — in a bid to rein in longer-term borrowing costs.

The extraordinary move comes as yields on Treasuries have been rising steadily over the past couple of months, threatening to drive up mortgage rates and consumer borrowing costs as the midterm elections approach. Interest rates paid by the U.S. government feed into all other debt costs globally.

But after Treasury's announcement , the yield on the 10-year Treasury went up, suggesting investors are unimpressed by this week's buyback, which was previewed last month.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is aiming to project strength as he looks to strong-arm the markets, which he says are incorrectly pricing U.S. debt.

articles.title: Microsoft has new AI privacy rules for schools
articles.summary: Microsoft announced a new agreement with the second-largest teachers union, the American Federation of Teachers, for AI safety and privacy principles.
articles.body: Microsoft agreed to a set of safety and privacy principles for AI in schools a week after two major school systems announced a ban on student-facing AI. In a new agreement with the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), the second-largest teachers union in the US, and its New York City affiliate the United Federation of Teachers (UFT), Microsoft committed to ten principles that can be contractually enforced by school districts that adopt them. The terms include pledging not to train AI models on student or educator data, limiting the amount of data Microsoft collects in the first place and disclosing to families how its tools work in plain language, prohibiting AI companions, and requiring human review for “high-risk” decisions. The agreement comes after New York City and Los Angeles both implemented one-year bans on AI tools for many students, giving the districts time to consider the proper use and guardrails. As parents and some educators have resisted the use of AI and screens more generally in schools, Microsoft likely recognizes that similar decisions could be coming. Beginning in November, school districts can opt to add the terms to new or existing agreements without having to renegotiate their entire contracts. The AFT, for its part, has been critical of tech in schools, but also open to working with tech companies to prepare for the current AI wave. In a May speech, AFT President Randi Weingarten called for a ban on screens before third grade as well as “student-facing AI” before middle school. But the group also announced a $23 million AI training hub for educators funded by Anthropic, Microsoft, and OpenAI. In a statement about the new privacy agreement with Microsoft, Weingarten said the terms were “iron-clad” and necessary “because no one else, including the federal government, has stepped up to do the real work.” She added, “We can get angrier and angrier, or we can act decisively; anything less than legally enforceable provisions is simply a wish list.”

articles.title: Supplements for dogs recalled over salmonella risks
articles.summary: Two supplements marketed for dogs are being recalled over potential salmonella contamination.
articles.body:
TOPEKA ( KSNT ) – Two supplements marketed for dogs are being recalled over potential salmonella contamination.

According to a company notice posted by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), New York-based Fi is recalling the supplements over an ingredient supplied to its manufacturer.

Fi’s manufacturer has stopped production while it investigates. Salmonella poses a health risk to both pets and people.

The recall impacts two dog supplements, which were sold directly to consumers and also distributed through online outlets Amazon.com and Chewy.com. They include:

Fi Calming supplement for Dogs 180 g Lot number – 26118 UPC – 8 50064 80011 1

Fi 8-in-1 Formula supplement for Dogs 180 g Lot number – 26159 UPC – 8 50055 11168 4

The company notice said salmonella can cause people to experience symptoms including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps and fever. In rare instances, salmonella can cause more severe health problems such as endocarditis, muscle pain and arterial infections.

Pets that contract salmonella may appear lethargic and display symptoms including diarrhea, fever and vomiting, according to the notice. Pets can also spread salmonella to other animals and people while appearing healthy.

People might become infected after handling the recalled supplements or by interacting with infected animals and their waste, according to the notice. Sanitizing surfaces that have come into contact with the recalled supplements is recommended.

People experiencing salmonella symptoms should contact a healthcare provider. Pet owners should consult a veterinarian if they have given the supplements to their dogs.

Federal health officials report that people who bought the recalled products should throw them away. For more information about the recall, contact Fi at 1-888-434-3647 from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. EDT or by emailing support@tryfi.com.

articles.summary: Amazon's Alexa for Shopping now lets customers verify suspicious emails, texts and phone calls against the company's own communication records.
articles.body: We have seen plenty of scams borrow Amazon's name, and some of them look convincing enough to make almost anyone hesitate. Prime membership is not required to use Alexa for Shopping, but if you are considering joining, see our guide on how to get a cheap Amazon Prime membership at Cyberguy.com. Now, you can also use Alexa for Shopping when something suspicious lands on your phone or computer. Instead of trying to judge a message by appearance alone, you can describe it to Alexa for Shopping. You might ask: "Did Amazon send me a text about a delivery problem yesterday?" Or you could ask whether a Prime membership email came from Amazon. You can even provide details about a phone call from someone claiming to offer an Amazon refund. The verification tool then checks the information you provide against Amazon's own communication records. How Alexa for Shopping checks an Amazon message When you ask Alexa for Shopping about a suspicious communication, provide details about where it came from and when you received it. You can also tell the assistant what the message said. Amazon then compares those details with its records. According to the company, its technology looks at information such as the sender and message content. It also considers timing and formatting. That gives Amazon an advantage over tools that simply search for suspicious wording or potentially dangerous links. Amazon can compare the communication with messages generated through its own systems. The company says it only confirms a message as legitimate when the tool has complete confidence. What Alexa tells you after checking a message The answer depends on what Amazon finds. If Amazon can match the communication to its records, Alexa for Shopping tells you it came from Amazon. It can also provide details about the communication and account security advice. If the message does not match Amazon's records, the tool tells you that the information provided does not appear to correspond with an official Amazon communication. At that point, Amazon may advise you to check your orders directly in the app or contact Amazon through its official support channels. You should also avoid clicking links in the suspicious message. There is another possibility. Alexa may tell you that it cannot verify the communication with certainty. If that happens, Amazon provides additional steps. You can submit more detailed information or use another Amazon verification option. AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS You can also forward a suspicious Amazon email Alexa for Shopping is only one of Amazon's verification options. Earlier this year, Amazon launched verify@amazon.com. Anyone worldwide can forward a suspicious message to that email address and receive a response about whether Amazon sent it. You do not need an Amazon account or the Amazon app to use the service. Amazon also offers a communication verification form through its customer service pages. So, if Alexa for Shopping cannot give you a firm answer, you still have another way to check before taking action. Amazon reports suspicious communications you submit There is another interesting part of the new feature. When you ask Alexa for Shopping to verify a communication, Amazon says it automatically reports that submission to its customer protection and enforcement team. Those reports can help Amazon identify developing scam campaigns and bad actors impersonating the company. That means the suspicious text sitting on your phone could potentially help Amazon spot a larger scam targeting other customers. Why fake Amazon messages keep fooling people Amazon scams work because they often start with something completely believable. You ordered something last week, so a delivery problem sounds possible. You have a Prime membership, so an account warning gets your attention. Then the scammer adds pressure. A fake email may claim your account has been locked. Another message might say someone placed an expensive order using your account. That urgency can push you toward a link before you have time to think. We saw exactly that pattern in the fake Amazon account email we investigated. The message used Amazon branding and warned that the account had been placed on hold. The safest response remains simple. Do not use the link in the message to investigate the warning. Open Amazon yourself and check your account. FBI HELPS TAKE DOWN AI PHISHING RING How to protect yourself from fake Amazon messages Amazon's new verification feature gives you another way to check suspicious communications. However, scammers will keep changing their tactics, so these steps can help you stay safer. 1) Watch for false urgency Be cautious when a message pressures you to act immediately or threatens consequences if you do not respond. Scammers want you reacting quickly because slowing down gives you more time to spot something suspicious. If a message claims your account will close or a package requires immediate action, avoid clicking its links. Check your Amazon account through the official app or website instead. 2) Never pay with gift cards Watch for anyone claiming to represent Amazon who asks you to buy gift cards as payment. Amazon warns that it will never ask you to purchase a gift card to resolve an account problem or make a payment. If someone makes that request, stop communicating with them. 3) Do not share passwords or verification codes Be especially careful if a caller asks for sensitive account information. Amazon says it will never ask for your password or one-time passcode over the phone. If someone claiming to represent Amazon asks for those details, end the conversation and contact Amazon through an official channel. 4) Do not trust caller ID alone Phone scams deserve extra caution because the number on your screen can look convincing. Scammers can spoof caller ID information and make a call appear to come from a familiar company. Seeing "Amazon" on your phone does not prove Amazon is actually calling. If someone unexpectedly calls about a refund or account problem, avoid giving them information. Hang up and check your Amazon account independently. 5) Use strong antivirus protection against malicious links Phishing messages can expose you to malicious websites and dangerous downloads. That is why I recommend using strong antivirus software on your devices. Strong antivirus software can warn you about known phishing sites and suspicious links. It can also help detect malware if a scammer tricks you into downloading something dangerous. Of course, antivirus software cannot replace good judgment. Avoid clicking links in unexpected Amazon messages whenever possible. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com. 6) Check scam reports for another clue Amazon also points U.S. consumers toward the Better Business Bureau's Scam Tracker at bbb.org/scamtracker. Amazon has partnered with the BBB so consumers can search reports involving suspicious communications. You can search using details such as an email address or phone number. However, a lack of reports does not prove a message is safe. New scams can appear before anyone reports them. When in doubt, verify directly with Amazon. Kurt's key takeaways We have spent a lot of time showing you convincing Amazon scams because they keep arriving in inboxes and on phones. Scammers understand that Amazon feels familiar, which can make an urgent message easier to believe. That is why I think this verification feature has real potential. Instead of staring at an email wondering whether the logo looks right, you can ask Amazon whether the communication lines up with something it actually sent. Still, I would keep one habit above everything else: go around the message. Open Amazon yourself. Check your account from there. If something looks suspicious, use Amazon's official verification tools before you respond. The more ways we have to interrupt a scammer's sense of urgency, the harder it becomes for that scam to work. But the cryptocurrency is trading around $1.36 just after 3 p.m. EDT, according to Coinmarketcap.com, a database tracking cryptocurrency prices. The coin dropped around 95…
articles.body:
Hunter Biden’s meme coin soared in value Wednesday before its price plummeted hours after the launch.

The $LAPTOP coin quickly surged from $37 to around $222 within its first hour. But the cryptocurrency is trading around $1.36 just after 3 p.m. EDT, according to Coinmarketcap.com , a database tracking cryptocurrency prices.

The coin dropped around 95 percent in value since its launch.

The behavior is in line with the typical lifespan of meme coins, which do not carry any intrinsic value but often surge in price because of social media hype around their launch.

Other political figures have launched coins — including President Trump and first lady Melania Trump’s meme coins, which similarly plummeted in value after their launches.

“But why would I ever want to support a meme coin? Why something that has been so misused by grifters? I understand the cynicism,” Biden wrote on social media the day before the coin’s launch.

“Trump has broken trust in everything he’s ever touched. And his token was no exception,” he added.

The coin was inspired by political controversy that has swarmed Biden — the former president’s younger son — since 2020, when the New York Post reported Biden dropped off his personal laptop containing incriminating information about him and his father at a computer store.

It fueled what would later become years of scrutiny from the GOP over Biden’s business ventures and personal life.

It was expected 1 billion tokens of $LAPTOP would be issued to its founders along with crypto wallet owners who lost money on Trump’s meme coin, subscribers to Biden’s Substack and people on a mailing list curated by a friend of Biden’s, Andrew Callaghan, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal .

Callaghan’s company posted a statement clarifying that Callaghan has “nothing to do with” $LAPTOP and that Biden was simply using a mailing list the company provided to “expand his audience.”

“As we have told our followers numerous times, we do not believe crypto is a legitimate investment,” the statement said.

articles.body:
Apple unveiled its long-awaited foldable phone, dubbed the iPhone Duo, on Wednesday, marking the technology giant’s first foldable smartphone.

The iPhone Duo will retail at $1,999, the most expensive sticker price to date for an Apple iPhone, and will be available on Oct. 23, Apple announced during its “Sunrise and Shine” launch at its headquarters Wednesday.

The iPhone Duo is a book-style foldable, similar to the size of a passport, featuring a bendable display. When users open the phone, they will be able to view two screens across what Apple says is the largest iPhone screen ever.

John Ternus, who took over as Apple CEO last week, said the new phone “will redesign the experience of using a foldable phone.”

“Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together,” Ternus said. “This results in a square screen that’s rarely suited for the way people use them.”

Ternus said Apple wanted the larger display to feel “as natural and intuitive” as the company’s popular iPad product.

“We brought together thoughtful design with breakthrough engineering in a way only Apple can, and the result is a series of remarkable innovations that we believe will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone,” Ternus said.

Apple said the display is 50 percent larger than the new iPhone 18 Pro Max and 80 percent larger than the iPhone 18 Pro, both of which were unveiled earlier in the presentation.

When open, a user can multitask on multiple screens, while dragging content from one to the other much like computer windows.

While the iPhone Duo is the most expensive iPhone Apple offers, the technology firm also raised the prices of most of its new products.

It comes as artificial intelligence fuels unprecedented demand for memory chips, which store and process data in everything from smartphones to cars to laptops. This has strained supply and driven up costs for various electronics manufacturers.

Earlier this year, former Apple CEO Tim Cook warned price hikes were “unavoidable” because of the demand.

articles.title: Appeals court hears bid to curtail access to medication abortion
articles.summary: A federal appeals court Wednesday heard arguments in a case that could eventually wipe out access to medication abortion, even in blue states that protect abortion. articles.body:
A federal appeals court Wednesday heard arguments in a case that could eventually wipe out access to medication abortion, even in blue states that protect abortion.

A three-judge panel of the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals peppered questions on attorneys for Louisiana, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and two manufacturers and distributors of mifepristone, a drug used in nearly two-thirds of abortions in the United States.

Many of the arguments focused on whether Louisiana has standing to sue, and whether the state had exhausted all its other administrative options before turning to the courts.

Attorneys for Louisiana argued that when the FDA in 2023 lifted a requirement that mifepristone must be dispensed in person, the agency infringed on the state’s right to ban abortion.

“There’s no dispute that Louisiana is experiencing 1,000 abortions a month due to ​mifepristone mailed into the state,” Louisiana Solicitor General Ben Aguiñaga said.

Aguiñaga argued that telehealth and mail access to the pills poses a concrete threat to the state’s budget, as well as its sovereignty.

The state cited two instances in which women who had complications after taking the drugs needed follow-up treatment paid for by Medicaid.

The state also argued that the Biden administration was targeting Louisiana when it lifted the restrictions temporarily in 2021 and permanently in 2023. The Supreme Court did not overturn Roe v. Wade until 2022.

At least one member of the panel, Judge Stephen Higginson, an appointee of former Presidentk Obama, seemed skeptical of the harm.

“I’m looking at six different steps … and we’re going to attribute that to the federal government?” Higginson asked. “There are too ​many ​independent actors to say that actually the government’s assessment of safety is what’s causing your 1,000 ​abortions a month,” he added.

The case argued before the New Orleans-based court is one of three brought by anti-abortion attorneys general from red states, challenging the legality of federal rules that allow abortion pills to be mailed to states where it’s largely illegal to terminate a pregnancy.

The Louisiana case has put the Trump administration in an awkward political bind: It won’t defend moves made by the Biden administration, but it also says Louisiana doesn’t have standing to sue.

Justice Department attorney Daniel Winik declined to stray from the narrow standing argument and made no argument about the merits — much to the frustration of the judges.

“That to me, I don’t find that very satisfactory that the agency won’t give an opinion on its own regulations,” Higginson said.

The Justice Department has been urging courts to put mifepristone lawsuits on hold until the FDA finishes a safety review.

“They seem to have taken a hard line, no engagement whatsoever on anything related to FDA’s process itself,” said Katie Keith, director of the health policy and law initiative at Georgetown University’s O’Neill Institute for National and Global Health Law.

Winik said he had “no idea” what action the FDA may ​ultimately take but that the agency should have final say.

“The whole point of our position in this case is that it’s the FDA’s job in the ongoing consideration of mifepristone to address all of these issues,” Winik said.

Keith said Louisiana’s argument about its own sovereignty undermines the premise of the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision and tramples on the rights of other states.

“This is much more about the states where abortion is lawful and access in blue states,” Keith said. “Louisiana has some of the harshest abortion laws in the country … and the idea that if you sort of change the [FDA regulation], that stops women from getting medication abortion in those states, is not correct. This idea that we’ll just make it illegal and then that will stop the activity, I think is not there.”

An administration official said in June the review is likely to take six months to complete, but initial results could be released earlier.

A district court judge in Louisiana set an Oct. 7 deadline for a status update, just weeks before the election, though it’s not clear how detailed the update might be.

The agency review is looming over the proceedings.

The Supreme Court has already blocked changes to the prescribing rules until it sees the case again, which legal experts believe is extremely likely to happen, especially given the various other mifepristone-related lawsuits.

After its review, the FDA could make changes sought by red states without court approval, but such an action would almost certainly be challenged in court.

Bella Pori, associate director of state policy at Reproductive Freedom for All, said the lack of arguments from the FDA defending the safety of mifepristone was expected but troubling, and it did not engender confidence about what she said is a politically motivated safety review.

“They were making a lot of procedural arguments about why this case should be thrown out of court, but … there are hundreds of studies backing up [mifepristone’s] safety, and this should not be something that a single state can question when we have all of the scientific data to back it up,” Pori said. “They chose not to make those arguments because Trump’s FDA is cowing to anti-abortion extremists who are demanding a baseless and unscientific review of mifepristone.”

articles.title: Apple Watch's new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple says its new watches won’t save raw audio, but features that can transcribe recent speech and summarize ambient conversations raise new questions about consent, privacy, and how people behave when they know they could always be recorded.
articles.body:
Apple is trying to get consumers to accept, and even welcome, a new reality: Your tech is always listening.

At Wednesday’s “Surprise and Shine” iPhone event, where the company introduced its new hardware lineup, the real surprise turned out not to be the foldable iPhone , but how the famously privacy-sensitive tech giant has decided its watches will now be able to process live audio and transcribe what was said.

Does this mean you’re always being recorded if the person you’re interacting with is wearing an Apple Watch? Not exactly — though it may make some people uncomfortable regardless.

It also raises the question of whether consumers actually want this technology, or if Apple forged ahead in this area because it was afraid that another company, such as OpenAI, would soon introduce a competitive AI device of its own.

Today, a number of startups are acting on the belief that AI-powered transcription is a key consumer use case for AI. So far, this more often involves transcribing meeting notes or recording lectures or interviews. Some companies, like the AI pendant Friend and Amazon’s Bee, ventured into other areas, too, with always-available AI companions that can help you remember your day by passively taking notes.

Apple decided to go a slightly different route. With its new watches’ “audio intelligence,” “Live Rewind,” and “Siri Recap” features, the company is straddling the line between accessibility and utility on one side, and what starts to feel like invasive technology on the other.

On its own, Audio Intelligence seems to be a useful feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, as it can alert Apple Watch owners to sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, babies crying, and more, using on-device AI. This can work even when the wearer’s iPhone is not with them and, in some cases, could provide life-saving assistance, such as when a fire alarm or carbon monoxide detector goes off. It’s doubtful anyone would take issue with this type of audio AI.

However, Live Rewind and Siri Recap move out of the assistive tech space and into a murkier area.

While Apple’s data protections may make these features more palatable to some, there’s still the possibility that normalizing listening technology may not be the best move for a privacy-conscious company. This is especially true given the broader consumer backlash against surveillance technology like Flock cameras , AI data centers, and AI apps in general .

For starters, the Live Rewind AI feature lets you go back in time 15 seconds and transcribe what was just said by double-pressing the watch’s digital crown. This transcription can then be saved to Apple’s new standalone Siri app so you can revisit the information later.

Apple suggests that this could be used to remember things like a “book recommendation, a colleague’s brilliant idea, or something you didn’t hear the first time,” but it also means that you can essentially catch anyone saying something they didn’t necessarily mean to have recorded and make a note of it.

This has implications around consent, not only from an ethical standpoint but from a legal one as well. AI device-maker Plaud , for instance, advises customers to obtain legally required consent before recording. Amazon’s Bee ‘s terms of service remind users that they’re solely responsible for complying with the law around minors’ data privacy, not Amazon.

Since Apple isn’t saving audio, it’s unclear how the court system might handle these new, text-only transcripts. It’s possible the notes could be introduced as evidence in court, but their lack of audio could make them harder to authenticate or verify. Plus, the evidentiary rules around their use will also likely vary by state.

Beyond the legal issues, the idea that someone can always record from their watch has cultural implications.

Already, recording devices have impacted the way people behave in real life, studies have shown , as has social media and data surveillance culture . Knowing you could be recorded at any time has a dampening effect on how you interact with others and engage in self-expression.

However, recording a photo or video still requires a fairly obvious move on the recorder’s part: you have to hold up your phone and face it toward the action. Snapping up a bit of audio to turn into a transcript just by pressing the watch’s digital crown is arguably a much subtler gesture, even though it comes with an audible chime and full-screen animation of a microphone, as Apple says .

Another new Apple Watch feature, “Siri Recap,” uses ambient listening to “take high-level notes” of your conversations, which can be reviewed in the Siri iOS app. These notes will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points based on what was recorded and summarized by AI. They will not be exact transcripts.

Apple suggests this could make sense for recording meeting takeaways or key info from a parent-teacher conference, for instance.

The company also tried to assure users that it has approached these listening features with respect for user privacy.

Apple notes that Siri Recap doesn’t default to always being on like some other AI wearables are. Instead, you can choose when it’s enabled, like only at work or only during the day. Plus, you can turn the feature off and on at any time from Control Center.

Notably, Apple points out that it does not create or store audio recordings, and that the raw audio isn’t accessible, even to Apple. It also doesn’t identify or attribute the speakers, and it protects the generated transcripts and recaps with end-to-end encryption.

Whether that’s enough for consumers not to feel like the feature is creepy is another matter. Either Apple has found the right balance between utility and privacy, or it’s about to see some consumer backlash.

articles.title: Read the Apple document explaining how new listening features still protect your privacy
articles.summary: Apple released a document alongside its new Audio Intelligence Siri AI features explaining how it’s going to handle users’ privacy and security.
articles.body: At Wednesday’s iPhone Duo launch event, Apple announced a handful of new Siri AI Audio Intelligence features, including Siri Recap, Live Rewind, Sound Recognition, and Music Recognition. Alongside its announcement, Apple released a document laying out how it plans to balance AI “ambient listening” and users’ privacy. It says the raw audio from the new features “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” Apple explains that Audio Intelligence relies on the Secure Exclave in the S11 chip that powers the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: > The S11 chip in Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 includes a Secure Exclave: a hardware-isolated compartment built into the silicon to process sensor data separately from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in the Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by watchOS, apps, the user, or Apple. Audio from the microphone enters the Secure Exclave of Apple Watch, where it is initially processed for speech, sounds, or music, without transcribing or storing the raw audio. This buffer is a continuously overwritten stream that exists only within the protected hardware and never creates an audio recording. Apple also says users control “whether and when” Audio Intelligence features are active — Live Rewind requires users to double-tap the Digital Crown every time they want to activate it. Additionally, if Audio Intelligence needs to be transferred to your iPhone, it’s transferred with encryption through both devices’ Secure Exclaves. Users also choose what text to keep from Siri Recap and Live Rewind, and text from Audio Intelligence will sync with end-to-end encryption if you have a device passcode and use iCloud’s two-factor authentication.

articles.title: Iran reignites Strait of Hormuz fight as US tightens squeeze
articles.summary: Iran appears ready to fight back against growing U.S. leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, and the threat of renewed war is causing oil prices to rise even as more ships are making it through the vital waterway with the help of the U.S. Navy. The Trump administration has worked to open passageways through the…
articles.body:
Iran appears ready to fight back against growing U.S. leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, and the threat of renewed war is causing oil prices to rise even as more ships are making it through the vital waterway with the help of the U.S. Navy.

The Trump administration has worked to open passageways through the strait and usher oil out, but the shipping lane remains essentially closed, and the escalating fighting is pushing oil prices higher compared to a more than monthlong lull in fighting.

Oil prices for the first time since July rose above $100 a barrel Wednesday — translating to an average of $4.22 per gallon of gas for Americans. And U.S. assets and allies in the Middle East came under renewed Iranian attack as the U.S. targeted Iranian vessels trying to export oil.

The tit-for-tat fighting between Washington and Tehran is only likely to intensify in the near term, pushing oil prices higher, according to Mona Yacoubian, director and senior adviser of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank.

“Ironically, the harder the U.S. pushes to get the strait back open, the harder Iran pushes back, leading to heightened escalation, fewer ships passing, and higher oil prices as a result,” Yacoubian told The Hill. “In other words, U.S. efforts to get oil flowing again by military means are having the opposite effect of further constraining supply getting out.”

President Trump brushed off questions Wednesday about American concerns about high oil prices, saying the aim of the U.S. war against Iran is to prevent the country from building a nuclear weapon.

“All you have to do is say, ‘Will you let Iran have a nuclear weapon?’ And the answer is no,” Trump said while speaking to reporters before he boarded Air Force One to head to the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas.

Trump added that he expected oil prices “are going to be tumbling downward” after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

He continued, “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”

Trump and his top officials have appeared to abandon outreach for negotiations and are trying to use an economic pressure campaign, a blockade against Iran’s energy exports, and military strikes to force Tehran to concede.

“Originally I wanted to make a deal, we’re so far down the line, they have very little country left right now, so we’re not looking for it,” Trump said.

He suggested Iran is holding out for a Republican defeat in the November contest to tie the president’s hands.

“Yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it’s not something we’re looking at. This war will immediately end after our election,” Trump said.

The president further warned that more attacks against Iran were coming.

“You’re going to see a lot more,” he said.

On Tuesday, U.S. forces carried out attacks on five oil tankers belonging to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), in retaliation for two ballistic missile attacks against a U.S. Navy warship, U.S. Central Command said in a statement .

U.S. Central Command, the military arm overseeing American forces in the Middle East, said it sank the Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island, with U.S. forces destroying 10 Iranian tankers over the past week.

That same day, the Treasury Department announced sweeping new sanctions against all of Iran’s airlines, claiming ties to the IRGC, and sanctions against nearly a dozen foreign entities for ties to the IRGC.

“The naval blockade now has an aviation counterpart,” Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies and a former senior Treasury Department official focused on sanctions, posted on social platform X .

The sanctions serve as a deterrent to any international bank, service provider or fuel supplier doing business with the blacklisted airlines and named companies — or risk sanctions from the U.S. themselves.

“While this isn’t a blockade in the legal sense and no aircraft is being intercepted, it does the same job through the financial system: it makes flying to, from, or for Iran very risky,” he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday the U.S. would continue targeting Iranian tankers in response to any attempts to strike American naval vessels.

“Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.

While Iran may not have full control over the strait, it absolutely retains the ability to disrupt shipping and will continue to do so for the foreseeable future.

But should the U.S. intensify its targeting of Iranian oil tankers, Tehran could resume targeting Gulf energy infrastructure in retaliation, as it retains its asymmetric missile and drone capabilities “and therefore the ability to continue to wreak havoc,” according to Yacoubian.

Case in point, Iran is responding with its own aggression, claiming Wednesday that it targeted 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz, including two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers.

The IRGC said it hit the vessels as they attempted to traverse through an area Iran declared off limits . Tehran also launched ballistic missiles toward a U.S. base in eastern Jordan.

The U.S. military has disputed Iran’s claim it struck the two American warships.

Iran’s Speaker of Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, also warned of more intense Iranian strikes against U.S. oil and gas facilities in the region.

“Strike our assets and you get struck,” he posted on X . “We’ve already proven it. Ask the bases that are no longer viable.”

In addition, Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, reportedly said Sunday that Iran is implementing a “restricted zone,” forcing any vessels in that territory to comply with Iranian demands.

Six commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, Reuters reported , citing data from Kpler. That is down from nine the previous day and below the 10-day average of approximately 12 vessels. Those figures do not include vessels that have turned off their Automatic Identification System transponders to avoid detection.

The strait typically handled 125 large commercial vessels per day, including oil tankers and natural gas carriers, prior to the launch of the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran on Feb. 28.

“All of this spells greater turmoil in the oil market going forward,” Yacoubian said. “President Trump is now saying that oil prices will not come down until after the U.S. midterm elections, an apparent resignation to the prospect of continuing high oil prices.”
