articles.title: US producer prices increase as expected in August; but key details firmer
articles.summary: By Lucia Mutikani WASHINGTON, Sept 10 (Reuters) - U.S. producer prices increased in August amid higher costs of goods, airline fares and hospital services, b...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept 10 (Reuters) - U.S. producer prices increased in August amid higher costs of goods, airline fares and hospital services, boosting the chances of an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve next week.

The report from the Labor Department on Thursday followed news last week of a sharp acceleration in job growth in August. Airline fares and hospital services ‌are among the components that go into the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Indexes, the inflation measures tracked by the U.S. central bank for its 2% inflation target.

August's Consumer Price ‌Index data on Friday could shed more light on the inflation picture and further shape interest rate expectations for next week.

"This report points to cost increases in the pipeline and will support the case of those on the Committee who want to hike rates now," ​said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics.

The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.4% last month after an upwardly revised 0.1% gain in July, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. The PPI was previously reported to have been unchanged in July.

Last month's increase in producer prices was in line with economists' expectations. In the 12 months through August, the PPI advanced 5.4% after rising 4.8% in July.

Energy prices increased 4.2% over the month as renewed hostilities between the United States and Iran boosted oil prices. Energy prices had declined for two straight months. Further increases are likely, with the benchmark Brent crude oil hitting $105 a barrel on Thursday.

Diesel prices soared 24.1%, accounting for ‌more than a third of the increase in the cost of producer ⁠goods, which accelerated 1.1%. Diesel prices are at record highs. Gasoline prices increased last month as did jet fuel.

"As the conflict with Iran drags on longer than many expected, inflation pressures are becoming increasingly entrenched, leaving investors in search of a catalyst strong enough to change the inflation narrative," said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial. "At this ⁠rate, a hike in rates next week appears likely."

Wholesale food prices edged up 0.1% last month after dropping 0.9% in July. Producer goods prices rose 0.4% excluding the volatile food and energy components.

AIRLINE FARES SOAR, HOSPITAL PRICES RISE

The cost of services nudged up 0.1% after gaining 0.2% in July. Despite the muted rise, the cost of transporting goods by road jumped 2.0% and airline fares soared 4.2% after dropping 3.1% in July. The cost of hospital outpatient care climbed 0.4% while inpatient ​care ​increased 0.5%.

articles.title: Trump pledges $500 ObamaCare rebate checks
articles.summary: The Trump administration is pledging to send $500 rebate checks to nearly 1 million Americans who the White House says were overcharged for ObamaCare coverage. In a recorded message posted Thursday to the White House account on the social platform X, President Trump alleged without evidence that the Biden administration was “massively” overcharging enrollees on the…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is pledging to send $500 rebate checks to nearly 1 million Americans who the White House says were overcharged for ObamaCare coverage.

In a recorded message posted Thursday to the White House account on the social platform X, President Trump alleged without evidence that the Biden administration was “massively” overcharging enrollees on the federal health insurance exchange and then hiding it.

“Our administration is doing the right thing and giving the money back to the people who were wrongly ripped off,” Trump said.

In a fact sheet, the White House claimed that former President Biden’s administration “accumulated a significant surplus of funds that were not used to benefit the Americans who paid these higher premiums.”

Trump said $500 checks would be mailed starting October to people in 30 states that used Healthcare.gov, the federal marketplace where people sign up for ObamaCare health insurance.

The rebate announcement comes as affordability and health costs take a central role ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Critics said the move was a desperate gimmick that won’t even come close to repairing the damage the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have done to the health system.

There are 19.2 million people enrolled in Affordable Care Act coverage, so only a small fraction will be eligible for the rebates. People who still get premium subsidies aren’t eligible, nor are the people who live in the mostly blue states that operate their own exchanges.

The recipients of these expected refunds are higher-income earners who no longer receive premium assistance after congressional Republicans, backed by the Trump administration, let the law’s enhanced subsidies expire at the end of last year.

Trump in the video claimed that “in many cases” the $500 would cover “the entire spike in your insurance,” which he blamed on Democrats.

But the loss of the enhanced subsidies caused many people’s premiums to double or even triple, prompting millions to downgrade their plans or drop coverage entirely.

Democrats shut down the government for a record 45 days last year in an attempt to negotiate an extension of the enhanced credits, but ultimately this effort was unsuccessful, and the government reopened without an extension.

Instead, Republicans promised to give them a vote on a bill of their choosing to extend the subsidies. The vote failed, and the subsidies expired at the start of this year.

Brad Woodhouse, president of the Democratic-aligned patient advocacy group Protect Our Care, said the rebate idea is “an absolute joke.”

“Five hundred dollars is a drop in the bucket compared to what Americans are paying because Trump and Republicans gutted health care to bankroll massive tax breaks for billionaires and big corporations,” Woodhouse said in a statement. “At a time when people are scraping by to keep up with the high cost of groceries, rent, and health care, this $500 gimmick won’t even begin to dig them out of the hole that Trump and Republicans created.”

The ObamaCare rebates are separate from the $5,000 checks Trump promised to give to every American if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate.

Direct payments to consumers are a key part of Trump’s health plan. The president has touted taking money intended for enhanced ObamaCare subsidies and paying it directly back to Americans to let them purchase their own health insurance.

It’s not clear whether every American receiving a check overpaid by $500, or in which year the overpayments happened.

The money for the rebates would come from what the White House says is a $500 million fund of excess user fees, which are paid by insurance companies to the government to help run healthcare.gov.

The fees have typically been used to cover services like technology support, call center operations and outreach efforts to enroll more Americans in health insurance plans. However, the Trump administration has slashed funding for outreach efforts.

The fee is a percentage of the value of the monthly premiums the insurer collects on exchange plans in a given state, and the Department of Health and Human Services updates the percentage each year through rulemaking.

The Affordable Care Act already has a mechanism for health insurance companies to send rebates to consumers who are overcharged, and it’s not known how Trump’s plan will interact with the existing function.

The so-called medical loss ratio rebate is sent when insurers don’t spend at least 80 percent of premium dollars on healthcare. The rebate checks in 2025 amounted to about $1.6 billion, according to health research group KFF. They were issued to 5.1 million people with individual coverage and 3.5 million people with employer coverage.

In the individual market, the 2025 average rebate per person was $233, while the average rebate per person for the small group market and the large group market were $190 and $91, respectively, KFF found.

articles.title: Multistate salmonella outbreak linked to broccoli sprouts: FDA
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reported Wednesday it will investigate a multistate outbreak of salmonella linked to recalled broccoli sprouts. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and state partners found 22 cases in four states. Two people were hospitalized for salmonella-related symptoms, and there have been no reported deaths. Washington has the…
articles.body:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reported Wednesday it will investigate a multistate outbreak of salmonella linked to recalled broccoli sprouts.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and state partners found 22 cases in four states. Two people were hospitalized for salmonella-related symptoms, and there have been no reported deaths.

Washington has the highest number of cases, followed by Montana, Idaho and Utah.

Salmonella is a common foodborne illness with symptoms that can include ​diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps. The CDC estimates this can start between six hours and six days after infection and can last four to seven days.

The FDA noted that this investigation is separate from E. coli and salmonella outbreaks tied to alfalfa sprouts and the ongoing cyclospora outbreak .

People reported feeling ill between July 6 and Aug. 26. The FDA reported that 89 percent of the 19 people interviewed said they ate broccoli sprouts.

Evergreen Fresh Sprouts issued a recall for its broccoli sprouts packaged in plastic bags or plastic clamshell containers. The CDC advised people not to eat, sell or serve Evergreen broccoli sprouts with expiration dates of Sept. 7, 9, 11, 14 and 16.

The recall was issued in response to Montana state officials also reporting a positive sample of salmonella in the sprouts that matched the outbreak’s strain, according to whole-genome sequencing analysis conducted by state partners and reviewed by the FDA.

In 2025, the agency carried out 26 foodborne illness outbreak investigations, the same number reported in 2024, according to the FDA’s website .

So far this year, the FDA has recorded 21 investigations into foodborne illnesses, with 12 outbreaks being reported since the start of July.

articles.title: ‘Super’ El Niño is now a near certainty. Here are 5 side effects you may not know about
articles.summary: El Niño doesn’t just impact the weather. There are five lesser-known impacts of El Niño we’re likely to see with this year’s super-charged event.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – The chance of a very strong, or “super” El Niño grew to greater than 90% on Thursday. In fact, it may soon become one of the strongest El Niños ever , the Climate Prediction Center said.

“During the October-December 2026 season, there is a 75% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950,” the national forecasters said in their latest release.

The climate phenomenon has continued to build strength as we get closer to a winter season peak. With an event this strong, we’re more likely to see the classic El Niño weather impacts in the coming months.

But El Niño doesn’t just impact the weather. Experts at Columbia Climate School recently broke down five lesser-known impacts of El Niño we’re likely to see with this year’s super-charged event.

“Now is the time to get ready,” said said Dr. Jeffrey Shaman, senior vice dean and professor at the Columbia Climate School.

El Niño doesn’t hit all crops the same way worldwide, explained Michael Puma, a Columbia climate professor and researcher, but when it creates extreme weather events, it can disrupt food production in a region.

While the outlook for wheat is looking better this year, the prospects for rice are looking worse, Puma said. El Niño is also predicted to impact the price of one major ingredient: sugar.

With many parts of the world already experiencing drought or unfavorable planting conditions, wild weather can make things even harder. “The El Niño signal hasn’t reached the major staple grains yet, but when it does it arrives in a market that’s already tight,” Puma said.

A Goldman Sachs analysis predicts the El Niño could contribute to a roughly 16% price increase in global food commodities. The World Food Program is projecting there will be at least 49 million people experiencing acute food insecurity by the end of 2027.

The picture is “similarly tight” when it comes to energy, said Kate Guy with the Center on Global Energy Policy. “Especially because we’re already in the midst of quite a tight and constrained energy picture and El Niño is only going to add to that, unfortunately.”

There’s likely to be more demand on energy infrastructure because of the need for more cooling power during hot El Niño years. At the same time as demand increases, some energy supply is threatened. Hydropower, for example, won’t be as abundant in the areas where El Niño brings reduced precipitation. Wind is also impacted in some regions.

Solar energy production may increase in some areas, but decrease in others, depending on storm patterns and cloud cover.

“We’re just going to see a lot of volatility across these markets and across these systems in the next year,” said Guy.

One possible bright spot: El Niño may bring a milder winter to the Northern Hemisphere, lowering the demand for heating energy.

We’ve already seen a major bottleneck at the Strait of Hormuz, impacting the flow of gas to markets around the world. Now, El Niño could create an environmental shipping bottleneck.

The water levels in the Panama Canal are already quite low, said Guy, and El Niño tends to make it worse.

“In past El Niños we saw the government really curtail ship traffic through the Panama Canal. They’re already starting to consider this, I’ve heard, and that could raise shipping costs and shipping times all across the world.”

El Niño is associated with a rise in global temperatures, which can be deadly — especially in cities. Urban exposure to extreme heat has already increased 200% since 1982, affecting 1.7 billion people, said Sheila Foster, a climate and law professor.

Most of the people who die from heat are indoors, Foster explained. Many have working air conditioning, but can’t afford to run it through heat wave after heat wave.

With a likely hot year ahead, cities should plan to fund cooling centers and give people relief from high energy prices so they can appropriately cool their living spaces, Foster said.

Disaster response in our country is generally built around the idea that there will be a single, isolated disaster, explained Jeffrey Schlegelmilch, a professor of climate and disaster preparedness. It assumes that when there’s a big problem in one county — say a fire, flood or hurricane — neighboring counties or states will be able to send in mutual aid.

But that doesn’t work when it comes to El Niño.

“El Niño is looking at a scale of disasters that are so large with overlapping calendars that everyone is going to be fighting over those generators in the power outage, or those flood control equipment or firefighting equipment,” he said.

The increased threat comes at the same time as we’re seeing a reduction in FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency) workforce and resources.

articles.title: Roughly half of hospitals complying with price transparency rules: Report
articles.summary: Even though compliance rates have reached a record high, only about half of U.S. hospitals are in full compliance with federal price transparency rules, according to a report released Thursday. The nonprofit group Patient Rights Advocate (PRA) released its eighth hospital price transparency report in which it found 49.4 percent of hospitals it reviewed were…
articles.body:
Even though compliance rates have reached a record high, only about half of U.S. hospitals are in full compliance with federal price transparency rules, according to a report released Thursday.

The nonprofit group Patient Rights Advocate (PRA) released its eighth hospital price transparency report in which it found 49.4 percent of hospitals it reviewed were in compliance with the federal hospital price transparency rules that have been in place since 2021.

With nearly half of all hospitals in compliance, this report marks the highest rate recorded by the organization since it began tracking in July 2021. There was also a 28-point jump in compliance from the previous report in 2024.

“Overall compliance with formatting requirements improved, but a substantial number of hospitals posted algorithms that failed to satisfy the ‘all necessary information’ requirement. Many of the algorithms were complex and opaque, preventing MRF users from calculating any price at all,” the PRA’s report stated, referring to machine-readable files.

For its report, the PRA reviewed 2,000 hospitals, of which 988 were found to be in full compliance with federal rules. Among all hospitals, only 18 percent posed dollar-and-cents prices for at least half of their items and services.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services “has made progress enforcing its hospital transparency rules, but this report shows that most hospitals still owe patients clear, usable dollars-and-cents prices they can look up before receiving care,” PRA founder and Chair Cynthia Fisher said in a statement.

In June, the Trump administration issued warnings to more than 500 hospitals over failure to comply with pricing transparency requirements. The letters included requests for corrective action. Hospitals that failed address these issues faced penalties of up to $2 million per year.

articles.title: Summer 2026 was the US’s hottest on record: NOAA
articles.summary: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on Wednesday announced that this summer was the hottest on record in the U.S. NOAA found that the average temperature for meteorological summer was 74.4 degrees, 3 degrees above average. August’s average temperature hit 75.6 degrees. Both were the warmest temperatures in the agency’s 132-year record. Most of…
articles.body:
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on Wednesday announced that this summer was the hottest on record in the U.S.

NOAA found that the average temperature for meteorological summer was 74.4 degrees, 3 degrees above average. August’s average temperature hit 75.6 degrees. Both were the warmest temperatures in the agency’s 132-year record.

Most of the contiguous U.S. experienced above or greatly above average heat last month, with near-average conditions isolated to parts of the northern Plains and the Midwest, according to NOAA. Much of the West, Southwest, southern Rockies, southwestern Plains and southern Florida saw record-breaking warmth.

High heat stretched across much of the Southwest, with new records set in New Mexico, Utah and Colorado, while Arizona tied with its past highest record. Daytime maximum temperatures also broke records as they averaged 88.6 degrees across the country.

Average temperatures in Alaska and Hawaii were both at their third-highest level on record. Alaska’s average was 52.4 degrees, 2.9 degrees above its average. Hawaii hit 70.8 degrees, 1.4 degrees above its average, according to the data.

The U.S. Drought Monitor also found that 59.1 percent of the mainland 48 states and Washington, D.C., were in a drought as of Sept. 1, having increased by 10.5 points since early August.

Drought conditions stretch across portions of the Southwest, Northwest, Rockies and Great Basin, having intensified in the northern Plains and part of the Upper Midwest, southern Plains, lower Mississippi Valley and the Deep South. It also found that more than three-quarters of Puerto Rico was in a drought, with more than 40 percent of the island in an extreme drought.

Temperatures are expected to be above average for much of the country going into September, with the southern and central Plains likely seeing the warmest temperatures. The West, Alaska, Northeast and southern Florida should see above-average precipitation.

Drought risk is also likely to “persist and expand further,” reaching as far as Puerto Rico, according to the data. The Northwest and areas from the Southwest to the central Rockies should see drought conditions decline, NOAA stated.

NOAA is anticipating the possibility of “significant” wildfire potential in the Northwest, the northern Great Basin, part of the Upper Midwest, much of the southern Plains and lower Mississippi Valley, parts of southern Florida and Puerto Rico.

NOAA and the National Weather Service (NWS) have seen drastic cuts to their staff since President Trump returned to the White House last year. He has also targeted NOAA’s climate research and the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research, with a leaked document from last year indicating that the Trump administration was eyeing eliminating the office and cutting 74 percent of its funding.

The Trump administration proposed zeroing out NOAA’s climate research for fiscal 2026. It has also reorganized NWS and made changes to its forecasting. Tom Fahy, legislative director for the National Weather Service Employees Organization, previously warned The Hill that these changes will impact how forecasters respond to extreme weather.

articles.title: US military takes lighter touch toward new targets in boat strike campaign
articles.summary: A year into its deadly sea-based campaign to stamp out “narco-trafficking,” the U.S. military is zeroing in on a new target — “floating refueling stations” — and taking a more human approach to sinking the vessels. Since last September, U.S. forces have carried out more than 60 lethal drug boat strikes and have killed more…
articles.body:
A year into its deadly sea-based campaign to stamp out “narco-trafficking,” the U.S. military is zeroing in on a new target — “floating refueling stations” — and taking a more human approach to sinking the vessels.

Since last September, U.S. forces have carried out more than 60 lethal drug boat strikes and have killed more than 200 “narco-terrorists” on both ends of South America.

In six instances of going after these larger refueling vessels off the coast of Ecuador, U.S. Southern Command (Southcom) — which oversees U.S. military operations in Central and Latin America — has reported no deaths of those on board.

Instead, a helicopter hovers over the water and U.S. Marines from the 24th Marine Expeditionary Unit board the repurposed fishing vessel to remove the crew on board, who are handed over to Ecuadorian authorities. And then the boat gets blown up.

The recent operations, which have been carried out with Ecuador’s blessing, mark a stark change from the direct hits — often shared in videos from the Pentagon — that have been described by critics as summary executions.

The new approach aligns with a more traditional law enforcement strategy in choking off drug smuggling in the Western Hemisphere, multiple experts told The Hill this week.

“First of all, the fact that the crews have not been killed in an act of extrajudicial violence is obviously a huge step forward,” Annie Pforzheimer, the former director for international narcotics and law enforcement at the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City, told the Hill in an interview.

“Secondly, the choice of the targets appears to be looking at the chain of drug trafficking importance, moving up further from the actual vessels transporting the finished product to a refueling node of the drug trafficking network,” she continued.

“And by moving up from the smaller boats that are moving products to a larger boat that is refueling others, you’re sort of getting closer to the people who are actually running the whole operation, and those are the people who are clearly more important and useful targets that you would eventually want to develop a legal case against,” Pforzheimer said.

The drug boat strikes, which kicked off on Sept. 2, 2025, have come under scrutiny from law-of-war experts , Democrats in Congress and some in the international community — arguing the U.S. was killing people without due process and violating international law.

The administration has pointed to the classified, written opinion from the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel that outlines the legal rationale to carry out the strikes, stating that service members participating in the attacks cannot be prosecuted.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged on Wednesday that the six recent interdictions — the first of which occurred on Aug. 28 — took place in Ecuador’s territorial waters and that the target selection depends on the vessel, the threat it poses and its location.

“These are part of the bilateral agreements we have with these countries, which is, I think, an incredible advance … for the first time, to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters, and then obviously we have to operate according to their laws in their territorial waters or their systems and protocols that they set in place,” he told reporters.

“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted; these routes are being ended.”

The deadly strikes on “narco-trafficking” boats, by contract, have been unilateral operations in international waters.

Asked why Southcom was still sinking refueling vessels as part of the operations, a U.S. military official said once a vessel is confirmed to be “actively supporting illicit activities,” like narcotics trafficking, “leaving it intact could allow criminals to continue or resume those activities.”

“Sinking the vessel ensures that it cannot be reused for criminal operations, thereby safeguarding maritime security,” the official said, adding that the operations are carried out under the U.S. and international legal frameworks “governing maritime law enforcement.”

Lee Schlenker, a research associate with the Global South program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said the new front in Southcom’s counter-cartel campaign is a “novelty” and a “welcome one at that,” considering the operations appear less lethal.

“I think it is very apparent that you can make the argument that this is more effective in going after the logistics supply network if these larger vessels are indeed providing fuel,” he said in an interview with The Hill.

A U.S. Defense official, granted anonymity to speak freely about internal military matters, said a fishing boat is “more difficult” to replace than a speed boat with three engines, but argued that both the lethal strikes and recent interdictions are “effective.”

“It’s like hitting a coca lab or sanctioning their bank accounts — all of them are effective at their respective level,” the official told The Hill.

Southcom has said in all six cases that the floating vessels were operating in support of Los Choneros , an organized criminal syndicate which emerged in Ecuador and was designated last September as a foreign terrorist organization by the U.S. government.

Several experts said they expect other countries, such as Colombia and El Salvador, to partake in similar interdictions with the U.S. military.

“El Salvador has been a willing partner, not just in sort of lending its installations and its civilian and military infrastructure for broader sort of U.S. operations tied to narco-trafficking in the region, but also for interdiction efforts that have been historic seizures that we’ve seen in cooperation with Salvadoran naval authorities in the Pacific as well,” Schlenker said.

Rubio said on Tuesday that Colombian authorities are working with the Pentagon on the new security cooperation and equipment purchases.

“In the end, the majority of this fight the Colombian authorities are willing to take on themselves,” the secretary of State told reporters. “They just need our help with equipment; they need our help with intelligence; they need our help sometimes with some specialized training.”

The lethal boat strikes have not stopped either. The U.S. military blew up an alleged drug-smuggling go-fast vessel in the Caribbean on Wednesday, killing three “narco-terrorists.”

Since unleashing Operation Southern Spear, U.S. forces have conducted at least 69 strikes and killed at least 230 “narco-terrorists” across the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, according to the Trump administration’s posts about the attacks.

The Pentagon has spent more than $820 million on Operation Southern Spear, according to a late July Inspector General report sent to Congress .

The Trump administration has branded the drug boat strikes as part of an effort to weaken, degrade and dismantle drug-smuggling cartels in the Western Hemisphere and argued the yearlong campaign yielded results. Southcom’s counternarcotics operations have reported at least 50 percent drops in illicit maritime activity across the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.

Experts are skeptical of the effectiveness.

Adam Isacson, the director for Defense Oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, downplayed the figures as “not that impressive” because there are “so many other” vectors drug traffickers can take.

Brian Finucane, a former legal adviser on use of military force at the State Department, said he has not seen evidence that the deadly boat strikes have reduced cocaine trafficking into the U.S.

Since President Trump’s return to the White House, the administration has designated 20 Latin American-based cartels and other criminal groups as foreign terrorist organizations.

Finucan, who is now a senior adviser in the U.S. Program at the International Crisis Group, said the designations are “something of a red herring” because those groups are not terrorist organizations the same way al Qaeda is.

“They’re criminal organizations, but they like profit, not political objectives, in which they use violence against civilians to further their goals,” he said in an interview.

Gen. Francis Donovan, the Southcom commander, told Congress in March that drug boat strikes alone “aren’t the answer” to the U.S.’s drug problems.

Pforzheimer, now an adjunct senior fellow with the Indo-Pacific Security Program at the Center for a New American Security, said one metric of success in the U.S. campaign would be making a criminal case to identify the entire cartel organization and tracing their money so that the leaders could be brought to trial which would “significantly disrupt the functioning” of the group.

Individual drug boats are “extremely” easy to replace by criminal networks, she said.

“Blowing something up seems like a really, really useless gesture because that is not going to stop anybody from moving anything,” she noted.

articles.title: Human rabies exposure cases on the rise, CDC warns
articles.summary: The CDC said it has received a rise in reports of human rabies exposure cases this summer, prompting an alert to healthcare providers.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — After a summer marred by foodborne illnesses , the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has issued a new, potentially alarming alert.

In a Thursday advisory , the agency warned health care providers of an increase in reported cases of human exposure to rabid or possibly rabid animals, and errors with the administration of responsive care.

Across July and August, the CDC reported a 17% increase in rabies-related inquiries compared to the same time in 2025. The agency pointed to “several high-profile rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events,” saying that they serve as reminders “of performing careful rabies risk assessments and following evidence-based recommendations for administering” rabies post-exposure prophylaxis care, or PEP.

Use of rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins is up 33% and 76%, respectively, this year, according to the CDC.

Health officials in Suffolk, Virginia, on Thursday warned residents that a raccoon recently tested positive for rabies within city limits. A dog in Mire, Louisiana, tested positive for rabies, prompting a warning from local veterinarians. In Elmira, New York, officials reported this week that multiple cats and skunks have recently tested positive for the virus. A rabies-infected bat was found in a Yosemite showerhouse earlier this year.

A bat in Raleigh, North Carolina, tested positive after residents rescued it from a lake , but health officials said the humans had minimal to no contact with it. Nearly 300 people in the state were also exposed to rabies via a mobile petting zoo’s baby goats, the health department said last week.

Rabies isn’t uncommon in the U.S. Roughly 1.4 million Americans seek medical attention after possible exposure to rabies, according to the CDC . However, fewer than 10 people die of rabies annually, a massive improvement from the “several hundred” who would die of rabies each year prior to 1960.

“Death is inevitable” once a patient starts experiencing symptoms, the World Health Organization warns. To avoid this, health officials strongly encourage anyone who believes they’ve been exposed to rabies to immediately seek care, which can include PEP. That process frequently includes washing the wound, vaccination and antibody treatments, which can prevent the rabies virus from spreading to the central nervous system.

It can be expensive, though, with costs running between $11,000 and $14,000, per the CDC. The agency encouraged health care providers to adhere to PEP and other rabies guidance in Thursday’s alert .

Others are advised to keep their pets up to date on rabies vaccines and to stay away from wildlife, especially those that are injured, sick, or dead. Bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes are most frequently implicated in rabies exposures in the U.S.

If you or your pet interacts with any wildlife, “particularly if you’ve been bitten or scratched,” it’s recommended that you wash the wound immediately with soap and water and speak with a health care provider about the incident.

Symptoms of rabies can begin with flu-like illnesses, including fever, headache, weakness, and discomfort, according to the CDC. If you were bitten, you may experience “discomfort, prickling, or an itching sensation.”

It can take weeks or months for those symptoms to appear. Then, roughly two weeks later, severe disease typically sets in, the CDC explains . This can lead to anxiety, confusion, agitation, hallucinations, excess saliva, behaviors like thrashing and biting, and being thirsty but scared of fluids.

Rabies was one of more than two dozen diseases the CDC paused diagnostic testing for earlier this year, but as of early September testing had resumed.

Nexstar’s Michael Bartiromo contributed to this report.
